rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence stops. Its best line, "whether Make's React output is production-quality or prototype-quality," is the adult question that decides the story; B's "what happens to junior front-end developers?" jumps straight to labor panic without labor evidence. A has a few borrowed assumptions, but B keeps decorating the launch into bigger claims the update does not support.
gaps_in_A: "first major product announcement as a fully independent company" is not in the update. "Follows the collapse" does not prove first, major, or company-defining.
"Designers Can Ship Production Code" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Make exports React and HTML/CSS from a Figma file; production readiness is exactly what still needs proof.
"Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io" imports a competitor set not supplied in the update. Useful research trail, but not grounded evidence.
"no IPO timing disclosed" becomes too much of a signal in the pricing angle. Absence of timing is context, not a live IPO story.
gaps_in_B: "what happens to junior front-end developers?" builds a labor-displacement angle from no labor data. "Automating a specific, common junior task" is asserted, not supplied.
"turns a prompt into an app" misstates the facts. The update says the assistant generates layouts from prompts and Make exports code from a Figma file, not full prompt-to-app generation.
"biggest bet yet" and "Figma's answer" to the Adobe deal collapse are invented strategic framing. Sequence is not motive, and no supplied fact proves magnitude.
"Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice" implies adoption and buying behavior. The update only says Figma is used at most Fortune 500 companies and the Make seat costs $25/user/month.
